B.Prabhakar, Hyderabad., vs Ch.Subba Rao, Hyd And Anr, Rep
Pp., on 21 July, 2023
The Hon'Ble Sri Justice Namavarapu Rajeshwar Rao
 Criminal Revision Case No. 762 Of 2016
Order:

This Criminal Revision Case is filed under Sections 397 and 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (for short, 'Cr.P.C'), aggrieved by the judgment dated 03.03.2016 passed in Crl.A No.34 of 2016 on the file of the III Addl. Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Hyderabad, wherein and whereby, the learned Judge confirmed the judgment dated 19.12.2013 passed in C.C No.623 of 2011 passed by the III Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Hyderabad, convicting and sentencing the revision petitioner to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year for the offences under Sections 406 and 420 and also to pay Rs.1,000/- fine.
2.

entities.text: III Addl. Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Hyderabad
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: The brief facts of the case are as follows:
The de-facto complainant is a technician in editing and dubbing and he started a business in the year 1997 at Hyderabad.
While so, the revision petitioner approached him with an idea to float a partnership firm and proposed to become a partner.
Pursuant to the acceptance of the proposal, they entered into a Deed of Partnership dt.07.12.2005.
The revision petitioner 2 RRN,J used to maintain and look after the business and the firm got huge profits.
Though the de-facto complainant repeatedly requested the revision petitioner to show him the books of accounts, the revision petitioner always postponed the same.

The revision petitioner without informing the de-facto complainant, started another studio in the name and style of 'Surya Technologies' and diverted the funds of joint business to the account of his business.
On 05.06.2010, when the de-facto complainant demanded the revision petitioner to settle the accounts, he threatened the de-facto complainant with dire consequences.
Hence, the de-facto complainant filed a private complaint before the Magistrate Court and the same was referred to the police to register an FIR and conduct investigation.
Upon completion of the investigation, the police filed Charge Sheet and the proceedings commenced before the Trial Court.
3. In support of the case of the prosecution, PWs-1 to 4 were got examined and Exs.P1 to P6 were got marked.
On behalf of the defence, DW-1 was examined but no documents were marked.

4. Upon completion of the trial and final arguments advanced on either side, the Trial Court found the revision B.Prabhakar, Hyderabad., vs Ch.Subba Rao, Hyd And Anr, Rep Pp., on 21 July, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/71775664/
1 3 RRN,J petitioner guilty of the offences under Sections 406 and 420 of IPC and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment as stated supra.

entities.text: revision B.Prabhakar, Hyderabad., vs Ch.Subba Rao, Hyd And Anr, Rep Pp
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Aggrieved by the said judgment, the revision petitioner preferred a criminal appeal before the Sessions Judge and the same was dismissed vide judgment dt.03.03.2016 by confirming the judgment of the Trial Court.

Challenging the above said judgments,
the present Criminal Revision Case came to be filed.

5. Heard Sri N. Avaneesh, learned Counsel for the revision petitioner/accused and the learned Additional Public Prosecutor for the respondent/State.
6.
Learned Counsel for the revision petitioner had contended that both the Courts below erred in convicting the revision petitioner though reasonable doubt exists in favour of the revision petitioner.
He further contended that the prosecution failed to establish as to who opened the company as alleged and even the bank account.
He further contended that the de-facto complainant was very well aware of all the transactions and he would also be in knowledge of the books of accounts being an active partner.
It was also contended that the complaint was filed in the year 2010 and only by colouring a contractual dispute in 4 RRN,J the style of a criminal offence.
Accordingly, prayed to allow the revision and acquit the revision petitioner of the said offences.

7. On the other hand, the learned Additional Public Prosecutor appearing for the respondent/State had contended that both the Courts below were justified in passing the impugned judgments as there is ample incriminating material available against the revision petitioner, more particularly,
Ex.P6, which proves that the revision petitioner diverted the funds to his account, which ought to have been encashed in the partnership account.
He also stressed on the point that DW-2, i.e the own brother of the revision petitioner himself strengthened the case of the prosecution.
Thus, prayed to dismiss the revision case.
8. The judgment of the Trial Court needs to be minutely examined as to how it came to the conclusion of guilt on the part of the revision petitioner.
Para nos. 18 and 19 of the judgment of the Trial Court would sum up its findings and are relevant to be discussed.

The Trial Court, based on the oral evidence of PW-1 and PW-2 who stated that the revision petitioner never showed the books of accounts to the de-facto complainant and with such reasons, found that the revision petitioner had a dishonest intent to cheat the de-facto complainant from the beginning.

After 5 RRN,J considerable analysis of this finding, this Court is of the opinion that the Trial Court erred in formulating its basis on such oral evidence in order to invoke the ingredients of Section 420 of IPC.
It would be appropriate here to refer to sections 415 and 420 of IPC.

415. Cheating.--Whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to consent that any person shall retain any property, or intentionally induces the person so deceived to do or omit to do anything which he would not do or omit if he were not so deceived, and which act or omission causes or is likely to cause damage or harm to that person in body, mind, reputation or property, is said to "cheat".
Explanation.--A dishonest concealment of facts is a deception within the meaning of this section.
(Illustrations are not extracted)

2 420.

entities.text: B.Prabhakar, Hyderabad., vs Ch.Subba Rao, Hyd And Anr, Rep Pp.
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property.--Whoever cheats and thereby dishonestly induces the person deceived to deliver any property to any person, or to make, alter or destroy the whole or any part of a valuable security, or anything which is signed or sealed, and which is capable of being converted into a valuable security,
shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.
6 RRN,J

A careful reading of the above provisions goes to show that in order to name an act as cheating, especially for the purpose of determining the guilt under section 420 of IPC, there must be a dishonest intention to induce delivery of property, which would result in some harm or injury to the person delivering such property.
Both the Courts below have not stated anywhere in their judgments as to the property which was delivered by the de- facto complainant due to the dishonest inducement of the revision petitioner.
The allegation against the revision petitioner is that he diverted the amount/profits of the partnership firm to his own bank account.
There is no element here to believe that the revision petitioner resorted to any inducement of cheating the de- facto complainant.

Learned Counsel for the revision petitioner relied upon a decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court reported in Vesa Holdings P. Ltd. And Ors. Vs. State of Kerala and Ors.1 wherein it was held that for the purpose of constituting an offence of cheating, the complainant was required to show that the accused had the fraudulent intention at the time of making the promise or representation i.e at the very inception.

entities.text: Vesa Holdings P. Ltd. And Ors. Vs. State of Kerala and Ors.1
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: There is no promise made by the revision petitioner, much less any inducement for delivery of property.

Therefore, applying the above decision to the present case, this Court is of the view that the Courts below erred in finding the revision petitioner guilty of the offence under Section 420 of IPC and the same deserves to be set aside.

10. Coming to the reasons assigned by the Trial Court vis- -vis conviction of the revision petitioner for the offence punishable under Section 406 of IPC, the Trial Court observed that the de-facto complainant entrusted the task of accounts to the revision petitioner but the revision petitioner committed criminal breach of trust by diverting the earnings of the joint partnership business account to his own account.

The incriminating evidence against the revision petitioner was admitted into evidence but the irregularity observed in the judgment of the Trial Court is, except the bank account statement vide Ex.P6 showing the credit of the two cheques issued by the AP State Film TV and Theatre Corporation Ltd. coupled with Ex.P3, no concrete evidence is on record that there exists another business in the name and style of 'Surya Technologies'.

entities.text: AP State Film TV and Theatre Corporation Ltd.
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Assuming for an instance that it so does exist, such grievance of the de-facto 8 RRN,J complainant shall be dealt with by invoking the provisions of civil law but not criminal law, in view of the partnership deed vide Ex.P5 and the version of the revision petitioner that the complaint was filed in the year 2010 only by colouring a contractual dispute in the style of a criminal offence can be believed and such attempts to invoke criminal proceedings in substitution of civil proceedings, especially in the presence Ex.P5 partnership, any violation of the same would only permit the de-facto complainant to protest by way of civil litigation.

3 11. More so, there is no clarity as to whether the partnership firm was active or wound up at the relevant period and the prosecution could not establish whether the above stated cheques were really issued in favour of the partnership firm or the alleged business started by the revision petitioner.
This being so, reasonable doubt exists in favour of the revision petitioner and he is entitled to acquittal from the charged offences.
12. In light of the above findings, the revision case deserves to be allowed.
Accordingly, the Criminal Revision Case is allowed.

The judgment dated 03.03.2016 passed in Crl.A No.34 of 2016 on the file of the III Addl. Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Hyderabad, wherein and whereby, the learned Judge confirmed 9 RRN,J the judgment dated 19.12.2013 passed in C.C No.623 of 2011 passed by the III Addl.

sentences.text: Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Hyderabad
are hereby set-aside.
Since the revision petitioner is on bail, his bail bonds stand cancelled.
The fine amount paid by him shall be refunded to him after the lapse of the appeal period.
As a sequel thereto, miscellaneous applications, if any, pending in this appeal, shall stand closed.
